questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to achieve the perfect balance between academic challenges and having time to explore the culture surrounding my destination. It was very important for me that my exchange wouldn't only be about strengthening my academic abilities, but that I'd also have time to have fun, explore new things and gain other experiences.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was an amazing experience overall. My only reason for not rating 10 is because of the general safety concerns surrounding New Orleans, which put a (small) dent in my overall experience. However, I think it is something everyone considering studying abroad in the US must take into account; the country is generally much less safe than Denmark.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy. The university was very good at communicating what they needed from us, what we needed to do before arriving etc., and it also sent us reminders if some actions of crucial matter needed to be taken. However, the Tulane website is a bit difficult to navigate, but as an exchange student, we received all necessary information via e-mail from Tulane's international office. It was therefore not crucial to know the website in order to get information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: No assistance

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The introduction program ("Intro to US Law") offered during the fall semester is amazing. It gave us all the information we needed to enjoy our exchange stay, and prepared us for the semester. We learned basic matters regarding studying law in the US, how to do case reads, basic foundations in different legal areas and generally how to navigate Tulane etc. Furthermore, we also got to do different "touristy" things, which was really nice to do as a group. I'd strongly recommend to take the introduction program, even though it means leaving Denmark earlier. Because of this program, all of us internationals also grew closer and became friends, which was a relief as the start of the official semester could seem overwhelming.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Find housing through the facebook groups "Tulane Classifieds" or "Tulane Univeristy (TU) Housing, Sublets & Roommates". It's easy to find rooms in general, but to find rooms that both have a fair price and are close to campus, is a bit harder. Be aware that many leasers/subleasers will be willing to negotiate the price, so don't just take the first thing you see.

Also, find a room close to campus, even if it means paying more. Public transportation in NOLA is not nearly as good as in Denmark, and it is generally much safer and nicer to live close to campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
If you live on Broadway St., you'll be living close to all the frats etc. It's a party street, so if you're not into that, find somewhere else to live. I lived on Willow St., which I was really satisfied with, but some of the other exchange students were surprised with how much partying was actually happening on Broadway. 

The houses have thin walls and you can basically hear everything that goes on on the street, if your room is close to the street.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university does not help much with housing, and it is not possible to live in the dorms etc., unfortunately. However, I was very satisfied with the place I ended up getting.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
When registering for classes, their system is a lot better than the one at UCPH. You basically create your own schedule, and can sign up for waiting lists if the classes are full. The system will tell you if your classes conflict (i.e., because of overlap etc.), and you can see how many students have registered for the class so far. The registration system is a bit difficult to navigate at first, because you have to learn how it works, but as soon as you've figured it out, it makes perfect sense and is super user-friendly. You don't "apply" for classes with priorities as you do at UCPH, instead you choose classes which have spots and register for up to 15 credits. You can add/drop classes up until 2 weeks after classes have started, which is really nice if you find out that there's a class you don't want to take, after you've had the introduction. 

Just beware of registering early for classes with few spots, as the waiting lists for popular classes can grow long. This is especially the case for seminars. Also beware of which type of exam the class will offer - if you're in doubt, contact Academic Services, they'll be happy to answer your questions.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always e-mail either the international office or Academic Services with questions, and both were very quick to respond.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted, except for one seminar which I registered for too late.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register as soon as the slot opens - make sure you've completed the immunization form before registration opens, otherwise you won't be able to register. Register for 15 credits, even though you only need 12, because you can always drop the remaining credits when you've gotten a better overview on which classes you want. Be aware of registering early for classes with few spots.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The academic programme was very fulfilling. There were a lot of courses to choose from and the professors were interesting and very knowledgeable. 

Also, beware that 2-credit courses do not necessarily mean that the workload is easier than a 4-credit course; the credits only tell you how many class hours the course lasts weekly and how much time you'll have for the exam.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: You can choose levels from 1L to 4L. I only had 4L which made it a lot more difficult, especially because I solely chose courses with legal areas I had no prior experience with. But that was my own choice. My friends who chose 1L courses had an easier schedule and workload.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is based off of the socratic method, meaning students are actively involved by using cold calling. However, the cold calling is used much more in 1L classes than higher class electives. The professors expect you to have read the cases, and be ready to present them and answer questions if you get called upon in class. Nonetheless, they're generally much nicer to exchange students, and will rarely cold call internationals unless half the class consists of internationals. I was only cold called a few times during my semester, and it was not done in a malicious way. I also had to present a case, but the professor told me beforehand, so I had plenty of time to prepare.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Antitrust
- International Commercial Arbitration
- Criminal Ethics Advocacy Seminar
- Insurance Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Professor Gabriel Feldman in Antitrust is a legend and made the course super fun and interesting! I'd also recommend doing a seminar, even though the workload gets heavy in the end because you have to do a paper of minimum 20 pages.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't experience this, but some of the fellow internationals received expensive medical bills just by getting checked at the doctor's, even though they had insurance. If you choose the cheaper insurance (GeoBlue), regular visits to the doctor etc. will not necessarily be covered.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books were much more expensive than expected, even if you chose the "used rental"-option.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university has a huge gym where you can also take a lot of different classes, which was fun. Furthermore, there are different law societies you can register for.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of different activities provided by Tulane, way too many to mention here. But download the app "Corq" and make sure to keep checking for events happening at the LBC, Rily Center etc., because there is so much stuff to do all the time. I remember the Global Café, Yoga & S'mores, free camping trips, rock climbing, workout classes at Rily, law bar reviews, free comedy nights, football games etc., just to mention a few. If you make sure to keep yourself updated, you can find something fun to do everyday.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do the law bar reviews, because they're fun. Sign up for some activities with the Rily Center, because you can access a lot of fun stuff for free that you wouldn't get the opportunity to do otherwise. If you have the time, sign up to a law society, such as the international law society.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel, travel, travel! Take advantage of being in the US, and travel around as much as possible. I went to New York, Las Vegas, San Diego, Gulf Shores in Alabama and Florida, and I loved all of it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It wasn't as difficult as I'd expected it to be, but the hardest thing was getting used to the safety repercussions. Coming from Denmark, it took a while to achieve a common sense on how to behave safely - either I acted too carefully, restricting myself more than necessary, or I acted too naïvely, thinking I could do the same things as back in Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Yes, just be outgoing and seek them out, either during social events or classes. I befriended a few Americans because I sat next to them in my classes, but most of my friends were other international students. Most of the American students are very friendly and curious about where you're from etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Danish social culture is much more reserved in my opinion, which made it difficult to adjust to the outgoing, "in-your-face"-American social culture. It could feel intimidating and exhausting sometimes, coming from Denmark, but it didn't take much time to get used to, especially because everyone in New Orleans is very friendly. I ended up loving the smalltalk-culture, where people aren't afraid of talking to strangers in the supermarket etc.

The hardest difference to get used to, was definitely the problem with safety etc., as I've explained further up in my report.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The fact that many people in New Orleans are extremely friendly and will help you out if you need it. They're also very direct, and if they find you annoying, you'll quickly sense it, which was kind of a relief because you didn't have to spend energy decoding social ques etc. In general, I loved how easy it was to talk to people and make friends, if you just pushed yourself out there and took the initiative.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Be open! Even if there are things you don't think make sense, try to take it as a new experience. Don't be judgmental until you've tried something, and speak to people to find out where they come from regarding their point of views etc. In my opinion, the internationals who struggled the most during the semester, were the ones who refused to go outside their comfort zone and only befriended other Europeans, people from their own country etc. Try to say yes to as much as possible, even if you find it mentally exhausting.

2) Plan your travels early on, so you have an overview on when you'll be gone during the semester. Buy the flight tickets early, because the prices will rise faster than you think. In general, if you have a tight budget, try to spread it out evenly during your stay; you don't want to make yourself go into debt, but you'll also regret it if you say no to many experiences, because you wanted to save money. 

3) Ask yourself how you want your semester to be (workload-wise) and choose classes based off of the answer. I loved my classes, but they were all upperlevel electives, which increased my workload substantially compared to some of my fellow students' workload.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1) Do not take the cheapest option regarding health insurance - take T-SHIP as it will cover you a lot better than GeoBlue. 

2) Use your professor's office hours to talk to them about their course, especially if you're struggling. Most of them are happy to help you out and they generally encourage you to seek them out. 

3) Many of the other internationals struggled with living with American roommates, because they're often younger and sometimes immature. In my experience, the people who lived with other internationals had a better experience than the ones who lived with Americans; problems such as what the AC should be set to, cleaning and noise habits often occured to those who lived with Americans. Many of the Americans studying at Tulane come from very (VERY!) wealthy families, and may therefore look at money, ressources etc. in a different way than yourself, which can be challenging.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Everything, to be honest. I loved meeting other cultures and learning about how law works in other parts of the world, I loved learning about the American legal system, especially because it is pure common law and I especially loved the weather in New Orleans. In total, I think I had about 2,5 weeks where the temperature dropped below 20 degrees celcius - the rest of the time, it was warm with blue skies and sunshine, which I absolutely loved. Finally, I loved the friends I made, especially because we are now able to visit each other in different parts of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting used to the difference in safety and academic levels. The safety issue has already been elaborated in the report, but regarding the academic levels, I would often feel a bit stupid during classes, if I didn't understand what was going on. However, you just need to accept the fact that you're new to the American system and it takes a while to adjust, which is ok. Again, the professors will gladly help you out, just make sure you go to them.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you're struggling with befriending people etc., please use the university's ressources. The university has A LOT of options which can help you out, and it's better to seek them out earlier than later. Remember, that the university is very wealthy, and you're not a burden if you use the ressources provided to you. If in doubt on who to contact, just contact the international office and they'll forward you to the relevant department.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
